newsitem.title: PERU: Long ordeal taking toll on Peru hostages.
newsitem.headline: Long ordeal taking toll on Peru hostages.

text.p: Hostages in the Japanese ambassador's home in Peru are showing signs of chronic stress, including gum disease and skin ailments, after 85 days under the guns of Marxist rebels, a doctor said late on Tuesday.

The 72 men, held by guerrillas demanding freedom for some 400 jailed comrades, are all in basically good health but are showing physical wear from nearly three months in captivity, said the doctor, a member of a Red Cross team treating them.
"They are showing problems common to people in captivity, complications related to chronic angst," the doctor, who asked not to be identified, told Reuters.

The plight of the hostages, holed up inside the mansion with the windows closed and no air conditioning during the hot Lima summer, has begun drawing more attention in Peru as talks to end the standoff have collapsed.

Local television said one of the hostages, Bolivian Ambassador Jorge Gumucio, had "an attack of hysteria" and calmed down only after being shouted at by one of the rebels. Several doctors have been seen walking into the residence in recent days.
President Alberto Fujimori's chief negotiator abruptly called off a meeting with the hostage-takers on Monday and there was no word by Wednesday when talks might resume.
Fujimori said he would exhaust all peaceful means to end the siege but hinted again at his refusal to rule out force if the guerrillas harmed the hostages in any way.

"I repeat and I insist that we will always exhaust all the peaceful measures at our disposal and we hope that the same contact is maintained -- that is to say, that there are no victims inside," Fujimori he told reporters on Tuesday.
For the hostages, the long ordeal is starting to take its toll -- as well as for the rebels, some of whom are also showing symptoms of stress disorders, the doctor said.
He had seen about 14 cases of inflamed gums, which causes serious pain in the teeth, and other dental ailments caused or aggravated by long-term stress, he said.

A few hostages have developed a skin disease that causes flaking on the arms and uncontrollable itching, the doctor said. He personally treated one such case but had heard of others, plus one case of unusual hair loss and another of psoriasis -- all associated with stress.

"We know these people were healthy when they came because they were all taken captive at a party, and you don't go to a party if you're sick," the doctor said. "The important thing is that all these ailments are being treated."
The captives seemed to be in generally good spirits and he had not seen cases of depression, he said. "The hostages are all talented people with great human qualities."
The siege began on Dec. 17 when the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels blasted into a cocktail party hosted by the Japanese ambassador and took all the guests hostage.
The rebels released most of the hostages in the first few days, including all those who had chronic medical problems or who seemed unable to withstand the emotional stress of captivity.
But they have kept their choicest hostages as bargaining chips, including Fujimori's brother Pedro, two of his cabinet ministers, the Japanese ambassador and a long list of Japanese businessmen.

Talks to end the siege peacefully seemed to be progressing well last week until the MRTA broke off negotiations and charged the government with planning to take the building by storm via a secret tunnel.
A mediation group arranged for the two sides to meet again, only to have the government break off talks, accusing the rebels of trying to backtrack on concessions they had already made.
Fujimori said he would not be drawn into revealing details of what form a violent takeover might take.

"Obviously the state cannot reveal what its working plans are, its strategy to handle this problem caused by the MRTA," Fujimori said. "I am not going to say if there is a tunnel or tunnels. I am not going to say if there are airborne commandos prepared or if we have commandos who could work with paralysing gases or other methods."
